newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bank fined in racketeer scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan bank fined in racketeer scandal.

text.p: One of Japan's top commercial banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd, was fined a maximum 500,000 yen ($4,275) by Tokyo Summary Court Monday for hiding loans to a racketeer -- the first time such a penalty has been imposed.
Court officials said the court accepted prosecutors' recommendation on the size of the fine.

The move comes ahead of an expected announcement this week of administrative penalties against DKB and giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co. Ltd, both entangled in a high-profile scandal involving payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.

The racketeers typically buy shares in companies and try to extort money by threatening to expose dubious business practices or are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings.
Payoffs to sokaiya have been illegal since 1983 but many Japanese companies have found it difficult to cut ties with the underworld.

Vice Finance Minister Takeshi Komura told a news conference Monday that the ministry's penalties would be decided within a matter of days, adding that the ministry planned to take stern steps against both companies.
DKB's violations of the banking law "severely hindered the ministry's supervision and also damaged DKB's standing among the public and was very regrettable," Komura said.
The police have urged business executives to adopt a confrontational stance against racketeers and spread that attitude among employees.

More than a dozen people, including top executives from the two financial firms, have been arrested in the affair, which coincides with the start of "Big Bang" reforms aimed at introducing more competition and global standards into Japan's long-sheltered financial sector.

The Finance Ministry on Friday filed a complaint with prosecutors against DKB and four former officials of the bank alleging they had hidden information about problem loans to sokaiya Ryuichi Koike during a ministry inspection in October 1994.
